summaries.example: Imagine you want to save your allowance for a bicycle. Each week, spending a little on candy feels like a good idea. But after many weeks, the small choices leave you without enough money for the bicycle. Each choice seemed enjoyable, yet the whole series worked against your bigger goal.
summaries.summary: Dynamic choice is about making choices over time. Sometimes every single choice seems reasonable, but the choices together lead away from what a person really cares about. This can happen because future rewards feel less exciting than present rewards, because different kinds of good things are difficult to compare, or because a person's preferences form a loop. A person may also have a large project, such as writing a book, that requires many small actions. Each small action can seem unimportant, but skipping too many can ruin the project. Philosophers study ways to handle these problems. A person might use a promise, a rule, a plan, or another arrangement that makes it easier for a future self to cooperate. The entry also considers whether firmly following a good plan is part of being rational. Dynamic choice helps explain procrastination, harmful habits, and environmental damage without assuming that people are simply ignorant or completely out of control.
key_ideas: A choice can seem sensible by itself but still be part of a bad pattern over time.
People may choose a smaller reward now instead of a larger reward later, even when they had planned otherwise.
Different kinds of values may be hard to compare fairly, such as spending time with family and learning an art.
Plans and helpful rules can protect an important goal from repeated temptations.
summaries.why_it_matters: Our lives are made of choices connected across time. Understanding dynamic choice can help us notice why good intentions sometimes fail and why small actions can add up to a serious result. It also encourages careful thinking about plans, habits, promises, and the way we treat our future selves.

important_terms.definition: A problem that happens when choices made at different times fit together badly and hurt an important long-term goal.
A goal or concern that matters across a long period, such as staying healthy or finishing a large project.
Giving a future reward less weight just because it will come later.
A choice pattern in which one option is preferred to a second, the second to a third, but the third to the first.
A promise, rule, or arrangement that helps your future self follow a plan.

questions_to_think_about: Can many tiny choices create a result you would never choose all at once?
When might a rule help your future self?
Is it always best to choose what feels best right now?
How could you tell whether a plan is helping or causing trouble?

summaries.example: Suppose a student intends to complete a research project by Friday. On Monday, taking a short break seems harmless; on Tuesday, postponing the work for another activity also seems harmless; by Thursday, the accumulated delays make completion impossible. Each local decision may be defensible, yet the sequence defeats the student's larger project. A plan with clear stopping points, or an arrangement that makes earlier work easier to maintain, may protect the project.
summaries.summary: Dynamic choice theory examines cases in which choices are distributed over time and a series of locally understandable decisions undermines an agent's larger, continuing concerns. One source is incommensurability: two options may be neither better, worse, nor equal, because their values do not fit a single determinate scale. Another is time bias. Discounting future utility can make a larger later reward attractive when it is distant but make a smaller immediate reward attractive when the moment of choice arrives. Preferences can also be stable yet intransitive. A loop such as A over B, B over C, and C over A prevents a consistent ranking and can expose an agent to a money pump. Vague projects create a related problem: completing a large activity requires many individually dispensable actions, so attention to each immediate choice can interfere with the activity as a whole. Autonomous benefit cases, such as the toxin puzzle, raise a different issue: the intention is beneficial, but performing the intended action is not. Proposed responses include changing incentives, using symbolic meanings, adopting plans, and practicing resoluteness. Philosophers disagree about which response is rationally required. The broader issue is effective self-governance across time.
key_ideas: Dynamic choice concerns the relation between local decisions and temporally extended concerns, not merely isolated acts.
Present bias can create preference reversals: a larger later reward is favored when distant, but a smaller sooner reward is favored when imminent.
Intransitive preferences can generate loops, including money-pump situations, while vague projects can be undermined by attention to only the immediate step.
Theories of planning disagree about whether rationality requires resolute adherence to prior plans, special incentives, or merely enough timely resistance to temptation.
Dynamic choice theory applies to procrastination, addictive behavior, and environmental destruction, even when no single decision appears disastrous.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory connects abstract models of preference and rationality with ordinary problems such as procrastination, habit, saving, and long-term projects. It shows why informed and voluntary choices can still form a self-defeating pattern. It also clarifies a practical question: how should present decisions take account of the person one will be later?

important_terms.definition: A difficulty in which a sequence of choices over time poorly serves an agent's continuing concerns, even though the individual choices may each appear reasonable.
Alternatives such that neither is better than the other and they are not simply equal in value; they may resist comparison by one common scale.
A tendency to give present satisfaction more weight than otherwise comparable future satisfaction, sometimes producing preference reversals.
A preference relation that fails the rule that preferring x to y and y to z should lead to preferring x to z.
A sequence of exchanges that can leave someone with the same kind of item but less money, because their preferences form a loop.
A goal whose completion depends on many actions, although no single action is individually necessary or sufficient for completing it.
A case in which forming an intention benefits an agent, while carrying out the intended action does not and may even harm the agent.
Firmly maintaining a plan when changing it would create a predictable pattern of failure or regret.

questions_to_think_about: Does a rational choice have to be best at the moment, or can it be required by a plan adopted earlier?
Are incommensurable options genuinely impossible to rank, or only too difficult to measure with one scale?
Does a money-pump argument show that intransitive preferences are irrational, or only that they are dangerous when acted upon?
Can a precommitment device improve freedom by helping a person pursue a settled goal?
When does taking a break from a project become procrastination?

summaries.example: Maya wants to improve her drawing before the school art show. She plans to practice for twenty minutes each evening. When evening arrives, watching one more episode feels more rewarding than practicing, and the art show still seems far away. As the show gets closer, she keeps making the same choice. No single evening ruins her goal, but the repeated choices do. A calendar commitment or a promise to practice with a friend could make the plan easier to follow.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of dynamic choice asks why a person's decisions can go badly over time even when the decisions are informed and voluntary. One challenge arises when alternatives have very different kinds of value. A beach trip and an art course, for example, may not be fully rankable as better, worse, or equal. Another challenge is present-biased preference: someone may prefer a larger reward later while it is distant, then switch to a smaller reward when it becomes available sooner. Stable preferences can also be intransitive, forming a loop rather than a clear order. Such a loop may produce a money-pump problem, in which a series of small trades leaves someone with the starting item but less money. A large project can create trouble in another way. Writing a good book or preparing for an event requires many small actions, although no single action is indispensable. Focusing only on the immediate choice can therefore damage the whole project. The entry also discusses autonomous benefit cases, where forming an intention helps but carrying out the intended action does not. Suggested solutions include changing rewards and penalties, using commitments, giving actions symbolic importance, and remaining resolute about a sound plan. There is disagreement about whether rationality always requires such firmness or sometimes permits flexible action.
key_ideas: Dynamic choice is about the fit between separate decisions, not just whether each decision makes sense alone.
A person can change her preference as a reward becomes closer, creating a conflict between earlier plans and later choices.
A cycle of preferences can make it impossible to rank options consistently and can lead to repeated losses.
Long projects require attention to the whole project, not only to what is most attractive at the current moment.
Philosophers propose plans, outside incentives, symbolic meanings, and resolute action as possible ways to avoid self-defeating patterns.
summaries.why_it_matters: Dynamic choice helps explain familiar experiences: putting off homework, spending money meant for later, repeating harmful habits, or making many small choices that damage the environment. It offers a way to discuss these patterns without treating people as either perfectly consistent or powerless. The topic matters because successful goals often depend on coordinating choices made by different versions of ourselves across time.

important_terms.definition: A problem caused by choices at different times that, taken together, fail to support an important continuing goal.
Options that are neither better nor worse nor exactly equal, because their values may not be captured by one shared measuring stick.
A preference for receiving a benefit sooner, even when waiting would bring a larger benefit.
A pattern where preferences go in a circle instead of forming a straight ranking.
A device or commitment designed to help a person follow an earlier decision when temptation appears later.
A long activity made up of many steps where no one step guarantees success, but too many skipped steps prevent success.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a future reward feel less important than an immediate reward?
Could two choices be neither equal nor better than one another?
Would a person with circular preferences always make irrational choices?
Is following a plan rational even when changing it seems attractive later?
What kinds of outside support can help someone keep a long-term commitment?
